practice_questions.text: Which design tool uses a diamond shape to represent a decision point?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: Flow chart (only). Distractor check: Mind map (no — uses branches), Wireframe (no — uses boxes/placeholders), Visualisation diagram (no — shows appearance without process symbols).

practice_questions.text: Identify one component found in a wireframe.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: any one of — placeholder boxes for images; navigation menu labels; content area boundaries; button placeholders; heading position markers. Accept any clearly named structural element. Do not accept colour or imagery (these are absent from wireframes by definition).

practice_questions.text: Outline what a visualisation diagram is used for.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks: shows what the finished IT product will look like (1) including colours, fonts, images and layout (1). Award 1 mark for a partial description that identifies appearance without enough detail.

practice_questions.text: Describe one advantage and one disadvantage of using software to create a design tool rather than sketching it by hand.
practice_questions.marks: Advantage (1 mark): any one of — easier to edit when design changes; looks more professional; easier to share digitally with clients/team; can undo mistakes instantly. Disadvantage (1 mark): any one of — requires access to the correct software; takes longer to learn; may not be available in all settings. Award 1 mark per distinct, described point.

practice_questions.text: Explain why a developer planning a user login system would choose a flow chart rather than a mind map.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (3): identifies flow chart is suited to showing logic/process (1), explains that the login system involves a decision (e.g. is the password correct?) with two outcomes (yes/no branches) (1), and explains why this matters (e.g. because mind maps do not show decision branches or process order, so the logic would be unclear) (1).
Secure (2): identifies the correct tool and gives a reason linked to logic or decisions but without full development.
Developing (1): names the tool only, or gives a generic advantage of flow charts without connecting to the login scenario.
Emerging (0): no creditworthy content.

practice_questions.text: On the page, sketch a mind map for a small IT company planning a new e-commerce website. Your mind map should include: the central topic; at least four main branches; at least two sub-branches on each main branch; and clear labels throughout.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8): central topic clearly labelled (1); four or more distinct, relevant main branches (e.g. design, content, security, testing, payment, user accounts) (2); at least two labelled sub-branches per main branch (2); labels are specific to e-commerce context (1); diagram is clear and well-organised with no unlabelled nodes (1); overall completeness relative to brief (1).
Secure (5–6): most criteria met; minor omissions in sub-branches or labelling.
Developing (3–4): central topic present; fewer than four branches or sub-branches largely missing or unlabelled.
Emerging (1–2): partial attempt — central idea present but very limited branching or labels.
0: no creditworthy attempt.

before.exam_tip_html: For the 8-mark “create” question you will be asked to hand-sketch a design tool for a given scenario — often a mind map, flow chart or wireframe. The biggest mark losses come from missing labels and diagrams that ignore the scenario. Use all four standard flow chart symbols if you draw a flow chart, label every branch of a mind map, and annotate every section of a wireframe. Examiners reward completeness, correct use of symbols and a clear link back to the named scenario — not artistic quality.

practice_questions.text: Which operating system is most commonly used on Apple smartphones?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: iOS (only). Distractors: Android (Google/other manufacturers), Windows (Microsoft desktop/tablet), macOS (Apple desktop/laptop — not mobile).

practice_questions.text: State one hardware consideration that affects HCI design.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: any one of — display type; display size; memory (RAM); processing power. Accept clear equivalent wording.

practice_questions.text: Outline why the HCI design for a fitness smartwatch must differ from the HCI design for a desktop banking application.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks: identifies a relevant difference (1) with a valid reason or explanation (1). Example: the smartwatch has a much smaller screen (1) so the HCI must use larger text and fewer data points to remain readable during physical activity (1). Alternative: processing power on a smartwatch is limited (1) so animations or complex graphics that work on a desktop may cause lag (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe two advantages of using a voice interaction method for a smart home appliance.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks, one per advantage: hands-free use allows control while cooking or doing other tasks (1); faster than finding and pressing a button, especially for simple commands (1); accessible for users with limited mobility or visual impairment (1). Award 1 mark per distinct, described advantage. Do not accept vague points such as "easy to use" without development.

practice_questions.text: Explain why a supermarket chain replacing paper receipts with an app-based loyalty scheme must carefully consider the HCI design of its mobile app.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (3): identifies a specific HCI factor (e.g. display size, OS variation, touch interaction method) (1), explains how it affects the design (e.g. the app must work on both small and large phone screens because customers use a range of devices) (1), and links to the specific scenario (e.g. shoppers use the app quickly at checkout, so navigation must be intuitive with few taps) (1).
Secure (2): two points made, one with explanation but no scenario link, or correct reasoning without full three-point chain.
Developing (1): one relevant point without explanation.
Emerging (0): no creditworthy content.

practice_questions.text: Describe four considerations a developer should make when designing the HCI for an embedded system in a hospital patient monitoring device.
practice_questions.marks: 4 marks, 1 per distinct described consideration. Accept any four from: display size must be large enough for nurses to read vital signs at a glance (1); display type — a touchscreen avoids the need for physical buttons that are difficult to clean in a sterile environment (1); processing power must be sufficient to update readings in real time without lag (1); keyboard or mouse interaction is inappropriate — touch or physical button controls reduce contamination risk (1); limited memory means the OS must be lightweight and dedicated to the monitoring function (1); the HCI must be simple enough for medical staff under pressure to use without errors (1). Accept other relevant, clearly described points.

practice_questions.text: Which data type stores only two possible values: true or false?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: Boolean (only). Distractors: text (stores any characters), alphanumeric (letters and numbers), integer (whole numbers).

practice_questions.text: Identify the validation tool that checks a required field has not been left empty.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: presence check (only). Do not accept range check (tests numeric limits) or data type check (tests format).

practice_questions.text: Outline the difference between data and information.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks: data is raw, unprocessed facts with no context (1); information is data that has been processed and given meaning (1). Award 1 mark if only one side is described. Do not award marks for treating them as synonyms.

practice_questions.text: Describe how an input mask is used as a data validation tool. Use an example in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks: an input mask enforces a specific pattern for data entry (1), for example, restricting a postcode field to a pattern such as two letters, a number, a letter, a space, a number and two letters — so 'SW1A 1AA' would be accepted but '1234' would be rejected (1). Award 1 mark for an accurate description without an example.

practice_questions.text: Explain why a hospital appointment system would use double-entry verification for a patient's date of birth, rather than relying on validation alone.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (3): validation checks that the date is in the correct format and is not in the future (1), but it cannot check whether the date entered is actually the correct date for that patient (1), so double-entry verification requires the receptionist to type the date of birth a second time, catching transcription errors before they are saved (1).
Secure (2): identifies that validation and verification serve different purposes with one clear explanation.
Developing (1): states that double entry is 'more accurate' without explaining why or what each method checks.
Emerging (0): no creditworthy content.

practice_questions.text: Describe four data types that could be used in a system that stores customer orders for an online clothing shop. For each, name a specific field it would apply to.
practice_questions.marks: 4 marks, 1 per accurate data type + field pairing. Accept any four from: text — customer name (names contain no calculated values) (1); integer — quantity of items ordered (whole number, no decimal needed) (1); currency/decimal — price per item (needs decimal point and currency symbol) (1); date — delivery date (stored in DD/MM/YYYY format for date calculations) (1); Boolean — gift wrap required (yes/no field) (1); alphanumeric — product code (combination of letters and numbers such as SHIRT-BLU-M) (1). Accept other valid pairings with clear justification.

practice_questions.text: On the page, sketch a data flow diagram for a small library that: collects member data via an online registration form; stores it on a network drive; and allows members to search for available books via a website. Include: at least three labelled processes; the storage location; at least two data flows shown with arrows; and a clear connection to the library scenario.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8): at least three distinct, labelled process boxes (e.g. submit registration form → validate data → store to network drive → search database → display results) (2); storage clearly labelled as network drive or similar (1); at least two directional arrows correctly showing data flow (2); clear labels on all flows (1); visible link to library scenario (member, books, availability) (1); overall completeness and clarity (1).
Secure (5–6): most criteria met; minor omissions in labelling or one missing flow arrow.
Developing (3–4): some labelled processes; arrows present but incomplete or incorrectly directed; limited scenario connection.
Emerging (1–2): minimal attempt, very few labelled elements.
0: no creditworthy attempt.

practice_questions.text: Identify one primary data collection method.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: any one of — email; interview; online questionnaire; online survey. Do not accept book, government statistics, magazine or website (secondary sources).

practice_questions.text: Outline the difference between technical testing and user testing.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks: technical testing checks that all functions work as specified, carried out by the developer (1); user testing checks that real users can accomplish tasks effectively, uncovering usability issues not found in technical testing (1). Award 1 mark if only one type is described accurately.

practice_questions.text: Explain why extreme test data is different from invalid test data. Use an example to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (3): extreme data is at the boundary of the acceptable range and should be accepted by the system (1); invalid/erroneous data falls outside the acceptable range or is in the wrong format and should be rejected (1); example: for an age field accepting 1–120, age 1 and age 120 are extreme (accepted), age 0 or age 121 are invalid (rejected) (1).
Secure (2): correct distinction made with a partial example.
Developing (1): identifies that they are different types without explaining how.
Emerging (0): no creditworthy content.

practice_questions.text: Describe two advantages of using cloud storage over a portable USB flash drive for a team of five designers sharing project files.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks, one per advantage: cloud storage allows all five team members to access the latest version from any device with internet access, preventing version conflicts (1); cloud storage is automatically backed up by the provider, reducing the risk of data loss if a physical device is lost or damaged (1). Accept other clearly described advantages linked to the team-sharing context.

practice_questions.text: Describe the purpose of testing an IT product and explain two effects of not testing it before release.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6): clear purpose stated (ensures the product functions correctly and meets requirements before use) (1); effect 1 described and explained with impact (e.g. if navigation links are broken, users cannot access pages, reducing trust in the product and causing loss of revenue for the business) (2); effect 2 described and explained with impact (e.g. validation errors not caught in testing could allow invalid data into the database, corrupting records and causing incorrect outputs such as wrong billing amounts) (2); well-structured, linked reasoning throughout (1).
Secure (3–4): purpose clear; two effects described but explanation of impact is limited.
Developing (2): purpose stated; one effect described without impact.
Emerging (1): vague awareness that testing is important; no specific effects described.
0: no creditworthy content.

practice_questions.text: Which type of malware displays fake security warnings to trick users into downloading harmful software?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: Scareware (only). Distractors: ransomware (encrypts files and demands payment), phishing (fake emails/websites), adware (unwanted advertisements).

practice_questions.text: State the difference between a black hat hacker and a white hat hacker.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks: black hat hacker gains unauthorised access with malicious intent to steal data or cause damage (1); white hat hacker is an authorised security professional hired to find and fix vulnerabilities before attackers exploit them (1). Award 1 mark if only one type is described accurately. Accept equivalent wording — the key distinction is authorisation status and intent.

practice_questions.text: Identify one type of malware that spreads automatically across a network without any user action.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: worm (only). Do not accept virus (requires human action to spread by opening an infected file) or Trojan horse (disguises itself as software; does not self-replicate across networks).

practice_questions.text: Explain how a phishing attack works and describe one way an individual can protect themselves from it.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (3): explains that a phishing attack uses a fake email or website designed to look like a trusted source (1); explains how this tricks the victim into entering sensitive information such as passwords or bank details (1); names a specific protective action with a reason, e.g. checking the sender email address carefully (because phishing emails often use addresses with slight misspellings), or hovering over links before clicking to verify the URL (1).
Secure (2): mechanism described with one protection, but link between them is weak.
Developing (1): phishing identified as a fake email without explaining the mechanism.
Emerging (0): no creditworthy content.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the impact of a ransomware attack on a small independent dental practice that stores patient records digitally.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8–9): detailed analysis of at least two distinct impacts with scenario-specific development; balanced consideration of both immediate and longer-term consequences; supported judgement on the most severe impact.
Impact 1 (e.g. data theft/encryption): ransomware encrypts all patient records — the practice cannot access appointment history, treatment plans or medical notes, so it cannot safely treat patients. This creates immediate operational shutdown, causing lost appointment revenue and potentially endangering patient safety if emergency treatment records are unavailable.
Impact 2 (e.g. financial and reputational): paying the ransom does not guarantee file recovery; regulatory fines may follow if patient data was inadequately protected under data protection legislation; patients who hear their medical data was compromised lose trust in the practice, reducing the patient list long-term.
Judgement: e.g. 'The most damaging impact is the operational shutdown, because a dental practice with no access to patient records cannot function safely, making it the most immediate and potentially life-affecting consequence.'
Secure (5–7): two impacts described with some development; judgement present but not fully justified.
Developing (3–4): two impacts named with limited development; no judgement.
Emerging (1–2): one vague impact; no scenario link.
0: no creditworthy content.

practice_questions.text: Describe two impacts of a cyber-security attack on an individual.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks, one per impact: financial loss — e.g. money stolen through fraudulent transactions using the individual's compromised payment details (1); identity theft — personal data stolen and used to open accounts or make purchases in the individual's name without their knowledge (1); emotional distress — anxiety or fear caused by the privacy violation and the effort needed to reclaim a stolen identity (1). Award 1 mark per distinct, described impact.

practice_questions.text: Which prevention measure requires a user to provide both a password and a one-time code sent to their phone before they can log in?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: Two-factor authentication (2FA) (only). Distractors: encryption (scrambles data, does not authenticate users), biometric device (uses biological features, not a code), access rights (controls what data a user can see after login).

practice_questions.text: Identify one logical prevention measure that protects against malware.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: anti-virus/anti-malware software (only). Do not accept encryption or 2FA (these protect data and accounts, not directly against malware detection).

practice_questions.text: Outline the purpose of the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act in an IT context.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks: the Act protects original creative works (including software, images and music) (1) from being copied, distributed or used without the creator's permission, requiring organisations to hold valid software licences (1). Award 1 mark for identifying protection of creative works without specifying the IT context.

practice_questions.text: Describe how encryption is used as a logical prevention measure to protect data.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks: encryption converts data into an unreadable format (ciphertext) using a key (1); this means that even if the data is intercepted in transit or stolen at rest, an attacker without the decryption key cannot read it (1). Award 1 mark for stating that encryption makes data unreadable without explaining the key mechanism.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the Data Protection Act supports an organisation's cyber-security measures.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (3): states what the Data Protection Act requires (organisations must collect, store and secure personal data lawfully and protect it from unauthorised access) (1); explains the link to cyber-security (this legally obliges organisations to implement security controls such as encryption and access restrictions, because failure to secure data can result in a breach) (1); links to consequence (organisations that do not comply face regulatory fines and reputational damage, so the law creates a financial incentive to invest in cyber-security measures) (1).
Secure (2): requirement stated and linked to security, but consequence or link to cyber-security is underdeveloped.
Developing (1): Act named and purpose stated without linking to cyber-security.
Emerging (0): no creditworthy content.

practice_questions.text: Discuss whether logical prevention measures alone are sufficient to protect an organisation's data from cyber-security threats.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8–9): detailed analysis of the strengths of logical measures (e.g. encryption protects data even if a device is physically stolen; 2FA prevents unauthorised login even when passwords are compromised; anti-virus removes known malware threats automatically); analysis of limitations (e.g. logical measures cannot prevent a determined attacker who has physical access — if someone steals a server, encryption must already be in place before the theft, and if they also steal the decryption key or the logged-in device, encryption is defeated; zero-day malware not yet in anti-virus databases will bypass anti-virus software; human error in setting access rights can still leave data exposed); analysis of how physical measures complement logical ones (physical barriers such as biometric access and RFID prevent attackers from reaching hardware; secure destruction prevents data recovery from retired devices); justified conclusion (e.g. logical measures are essential but insufficient alone — a layered approach combining physical, logical and procedural controls provides the strongest protection).
Secure (5–7): both sides addressed with some development; conclusion present but not fully justified.
Developing (3–4): logical measures described with some limitations noted; one-sided.
Emerging (1–2): vague awareness that both types of measure exist; no analysis.
0: no creditworthy content.

practice_questions.text: On the page, sketch a diagram showing how a small restaurant could use digital communications to promote a new menu to local customers. Your diagram should include: the communication type(s) chosen; the software or device used to create and send them; the distribution channel(s); the connectivity method; and a clear link to the local restaurant scenario throughout.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8): at least two labelled communication types appropriate to a local restaurant (e.g. social media post, email newsletter, website update) (1); software or device labelled for each (e.g. smartphone app for social media, PC with office software for newsletter) (2); distribution channel labelled for each type (e.g. social media platform, email, website) (1); connectivity method included (e.g. Wi-Fi or mobile data/4G) (1); clear directional flow from creation to audience (1); all elements linked to local restaurant scenario (1); overall completeness and clarity (1).
Secure (5–6): most criteria met; minor omissions in connectivity or scenario links.
Developing (3–4): some labelled elements; distribution channel or connectivity missing.
Emerging (1–2): minimal labelled attempt.
0: no creditworthy attempt.

practice_questions.text: State one advantage of using video as a digital communication type.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: any one of — highly engaging because it combines visuals, audio and motion (1); effective for demonstrating a product or process step by step (1); easy to share across social media and multimedia platforms, reaching a large audience quickly (1). Accept any clearly stated, relevant advantage.

practice_questions.text: Describe two characteristics of a smartphone that make it suitable for distributing digital communications to a mobile audience.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks, one per characteristic: portable — users carry it constantly, so they receive push notifications and messages at any time and place (1); connected to 4G/5G mobile networks — the user can access content even without a Wi-Fi connection, making it suitable for audiences on the move (1). Accept other clearly described relevant characteristics such as touchscreen interaction or built-in camera for content creation.

practice_questions.text: Explain why a charity targeting elderly donors in rural areas might choose email distribution over social media distribution.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (3): identifies a relevant demographic factor (age — older users are less likely to use social media platforms) (1); explains this in context (so email is more likely to reach the intended audience because older users are familiar with and regularly check email) (1); adds a second supporting reason (rural location means mobile data coverage may be weaker, but email works reliably over a wired home broadband connection that rural users are more likely to have than consistent 4G/5G) (1).
Secure (2): two points, one with explanation but not fully developed.
Developing (1): names email and social media with a vague reference to age without explaining why.
Emerging (0): no creditworthy content.

practice_questions.text: Outline the difference between Desktop Publishing software and standard office applications for creating digital communications.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks: DTP software is designed specifically for layout-intensive documents and offers precise control over typography, image placement and colour (1); standard office applications are more widely available and familiar to users but offer less design control and are better suited to documents where structure and content are more important than precise visual design (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe four factors a digital marketing team should consider when selecting a distribution channel and connectivity method for a campaign targeting 16–24-year-old students in a city.
practice_questions.marks: 4 marks, 1 per described factor linked to the demographic. Accept any four: age — 16–24-year-olds heavily use mobile apps and social media platforms, so a mobile app or social media channel is appropriate (1); location (urban) — strong 4G/5G and Wi-Fi coverage in cities means mobile data or Wi-Fi connectivity will work reliably, enabling video and interactive content (1); device preference — this demographic predominantly uses smartphones, so the channel must be mobile-optimised with app notifications or social media feeds (1); accessibility — ensure content has captions or alternative text for students who rely on assistive technology (1); cost — students may use free platforms rather than subscribing to services, so free distribution channels (social media, website) are more likely to reach them (1). Award marks for any four clearly described, context-linked factors.

practice_questions.text: Which of the following is NOT one of the four pillars of the Internet of Everything?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: Software (only). Distractors: People, process, data and things (all IoE pillars).

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by device-to-device interaction in an IoE system.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: automated communication between two or more connected devices without human involvement (accept equivalent clear description). Do not accept human-to-device interaction.

practice_questions.text: Describe one advantage and one disadvantage of using IoE in health monitoring.
practice_questions.marks: Advantage (1 mark): any one of — wearable devices monitor vital signs continuously, enabling early detection of health problems without the patient visiting a clinic; remote monitoring reduces pressure on hospital resources by allowing patients with chronic conditions to be tracked at home. Disadvantage (1 mark): any one of — health data transmitted wirelessly is sensitive and could be intercepted by attackers, risking privacy and potentially enabling identity theft; dependence on internet connectivity means monitoring fails if the connection is lost, which could be dangerous in a critical care context. Award 1 mark per distinct, described point.

practice_questions.text: Explain why a smart city traffic management system using IoE is vulnerable to cyber-security attacks, and describe one potential consequence.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (3): explains that every connected device (traffic sensors, traffic lights, road signs) is an attack surface (1); explains the specific vulnerability (an attacker could intercept or modify traffic signal data, causing congestion or dangerous signal failures) (1); describes a specific consequence (e.g. emergency vehicles delayed because traffic light control is disrupted, leading to slower response times and potential harm) (1).
Secure (2): vulnerability identified with one consequence, but the chain of reasoning is incomplete.
Developing (1): states that IoE has security risks without linking to the traffic management context.
Emerging (0): no creditworthy content.

practice_questions.text: Describe how IoE is used in manufacturing to improve efficiency.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks: sensors on machinery monitor performance data in real time (1); this data is processed to detect early signs of wear or failure, allowing maintenance to be scheduled before a breakdown occurs (predictive maintenance), reducing costly unplanned downtime and keeping the production line running (1). Award 1 mark for mentioning sensors or automation without describing how the data is used to improve efficiency.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the benefits and security risks of introducing IoE smart devices into an NHS hospital. In your answer, consider the impact on both patients and the organisation.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8–9): detailed analysis of at least two benefits (e.g. continuous remote monitoring of patient vital signs via wearable sensors reduces unnecessary hospital admissions and enables faster clinical responses; device-to-device interaction between medical equipment and consultant devices means specialists can monitor multiple patients simultaneously without physical presence); detailed analysis of at least two security risks (e.g. medical devices with weak security are attack surfaces — an attacker compromising a connected infusion pump or patient monitor could manipulate data, leading to incorrect treatment decisions and patient harm; interception of transmitted patient data violates data protection legislation and could expose sensitive medical records, resulting in regulatory fines and loss of patient trust); balanced judgement with justification (e.g. 'The security risks are particularly severe in a hospital context because any system failure or data manipulation could directly endanger patient safety, making robust cyber-security measures — such as encryption of all device transmissions and strict access rights — essential before IoE benefits can be safely realised.').
Secure (5–7): two benefits and two risks described with some development; judgement present but not fully justified or lacking clear scenario link.
Developing (3–4): benefits and risks named with limited development; no judgement.
Emerging (1–2): one vague benefit or risk; no scenario link or analysis.
0: no creditworthy content.

practice_questions.text: Which display type uses almost no power and is highly readable in direct sunlight, making it suitable for outdoor information screens?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: e-ink (only). Distractors: LCD (requires backlight, less readable in sunlight), OLED (power-hungry per pixel, reflective in bright light), capacitive touchscreen (a touch input method, not a display technology in the same sense).

practice_questions.text: State one difference between RAM and storage.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: accept any one accurate contrast, e.g. RAM is temporary (wiped when the device powers off) whereas storage is permanent (data remains after shutdown) (1); OR RAM holds actively running data whereas storage holds saved files and installed applications (1); OR RAM affects processing speed and responsiveness whereas storage determines how much data can be saved (1).

practice_questions.text: Outline how display size affects the design of an HCI for a smartwatch compared with a desktop monitor.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks: smartwatch screens are very small (1–2 inches) so the HCI must use large icons, minimal text and simple gestures because little content fits on screen at once (1); desktop monitor screens are large (13–34 inches) and support multi-column layouts, dense menus and detailed dashboards because much more content can be shown simultaneously (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe how insufficient RAM affects the user experience of an HCI. Give an example in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks: RAM holds the data and instructions being actively processed by the device; if there is insufficient RAM, the processor cannot hold all required data in working memory simultaneously (1), causing the HCI to slow down, animations to stutter or apps to crash — for example, a banking app with multiple open tabs and real-time balance updates may freeze if the device runs out of RAM (1). Award 1 mark for correctly identifying RAM as working/temporary memory without linking to the user experience impact.

practice_questions.text: Explain how processing power affects the design decisions a developer makes when creating an HCI for an embedded system in a domestic appliance compared with a financial trading dashboard.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (3): identifies that embedded systems in domestic appliances have low processing power, so the HCI must be simple and lightweight — minimal graphics, few options, no animations — because the processor cannot execute complex instructions quickly (1); a financial trading dashboard runs on a high-powered desktop system and can therefore support real-time charts, animated data visualisations and multiple simultaneous background processes (1); concludes that processing power directly constrains design complexity — the designer must not include features the available processor cannot execute within an acceptable response time (1).
Secure (2): two of the three mark points developed; link between processing power and design decisions partially explained.
Developing (1): states that more processing power enables a 'better' interface without explaining the specific design consequences.
Emerging (0): no creditworthy content.

practice_questions.text: A designer is creating an HCI for a self-service checkout terminal in a supermarket. The terminal uses a capacitive touchscreen and must process transactions, display product information and manage a receipt printer simultaneously. Sketch a comparison of the hardware considerations for this terminal versus a wearable fitness tracker. In your sketch, address display type, display size, RAM and processing power for each device. Justify each hardware choice.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8): sketch or structured response clearly addresses all four hardware considerations for both devices (1 per consideration per device = up to 8, capped at 8). For the self-service terminal: large capacitive touchscreen (accessible touch interaction for diverse users, transaction input) (1); large display (55+ cm, product images visible from normal standing distance) (1); sufficient RAM to run payment processing, product database queries and peripheral control simultaneously without lag (1); adequate processing power for real-time transaction handling and fast UI responses to prevent queue build-up (1). For the fitness tracker: small OLED or LCD touchscreen (compact, visible in varied lighting, low profile on wrist) (1); small display (2–3 cm, shows only key metrics: steps, heart rate) (1); minimal RAM (single-purpose device, tracks one or two data streams) (1); low processing power (battery life is the priority; complex calculations are sent to the paired smartphone) (1). Accept reasonable alternative justified choices.
Secure (5–6): most considerations addressed for both devices with clear justification; one or two gaps.
Developing (3–4): addresses hardware for one device in depth or covers all four considerations without justification.
Emerging (1–2): names hardware components with no contextual justification.
0: no creditworthy content.

practice_questions.text: Which operating system runs on Chromebook laptops and supports web applications as well as Android apps on compatible devices?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: Chrome OS (only). Distractors: Windows (uses locally installed applications), Ubuntu (Linux distribution, not browser-based by default), iOS (mobile OS, not found on laptops).

practice_questions.text: Identify one key difference between iOS and Android as mobile operating systems.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: accept any one accurate contrast, e.g. App Store apps must pass Apple review, although some regions allow alternative distribution (1); OR Android is open-source and runs on devices from many different manufacturers, whereas iOS runs only on Apple devices (1); OR Android is used on a wider range of screen sizes and hardware specs, requiring designers to plan for more variation (1).

practice_questions.text: Outline how the operating system choice affects HCI design for a developer creating a productivity application.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks: each OS has its own design conventions and interaction patterns (1); for example, Windows users expect resizable windows and keyboard shortcuts while iOS users expect swipe gestures and a specific bottom navigation bar, so the designer must follow the target OS conventions or the HCI will feel unfamiliar and be harder to use (1). Accept other valid OS-specific examples.

practice_questions.text: Describe the characteristics of a database as a digital platform, and explain why it suits a professional data entry context.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks: a database platform presents data in structured tables and forms with search, filter and data entry controls (1); this suits professional data entry because users need to retrieve specific records quickly, enter validated data accurately and view multiple related fields simultaneously — tasks the database HCI is specifically designed to support (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain how the operating system affects the HCI design choices available to a developer creating an interface for Android compared with iOS.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (3): identifies that Android is open-source and runs on devices from many manufacturers with varying screen sizes and hardware specifications (1); explains the HCI design consequence: the developer must create responsive layouts that adapt to different screen dimensions and cannot assume a consistent hardware baseline (1); contrasts with iOS: the closed ecosystem and strict Human Interface Guidelines constrain design choices but mean the developer can target fewer device variants with a more controlled visual standard (1).
Secure (2): OS difference stated and one clear HCI design consequence explained; second platform underdeveloped.
Developing (1): identifies that the two platforms differ without explaining specific HCI design implications.
Emerging (0): no creditworthy content.

practice_questions.text: Sketch a mapping of the eight operating systems to their primary device types and use contexts. For each OS, note one HCI design implication.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8): sketch or structured table identifies all eight OS entries (Windows, macOS, iOS, Android, Chrome OS, Ubuntu, Linux, Unix) with accurate primary device type and at least one HCI implication for each. Sample answers: Windows — business/education desktop, taskbar + Start menu conventions, mouse and keyboard input (1); macOS — Apple hardware only, Dock + menu bar, polished visual guidelines (1); iOS — iPhone/iPad, closed App Store, swipe gestures, consistent nav conventions (1); Android — multi-manufacturer smartphones, open-source, responsive layouts needed across device sizes (1); Chrome OS — Chromebook, browser-based apps, web-first responsive design (1); Ubuntu — user-friendly Linux on desktops, graphical desktop similar to Windows but highly configurable (1); Linux — servers/developer machines, command-line primary, minimal graphical HCI (1); Unix — enterprise/academic servers, command-line interface, rarely the target of consumer HCI (1).
Secure (5–6): six or seven OS entries with accurate types and implications.
Developing (3–4): four or five entries; some implications missing or inaccurate.
Emerging (1–2): fewer than four entries; implications largely absent.
0: no creditworthy content.

practice_questions.text: Which digital device is best suited to group viewing across a room in a classroom setting, where all participants must be able to see the content simultaneously?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: smartboard (only). Distractors: smartphone (small screen, individual use), tablet (small screen, individual use), PC/laptop (typically single-user, screen not large enough for group viewing across a room).

practice_questions.text: Identify one accessibility need that would make a smartphone an unsuitable device for a user.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: accept any one valid accessibility need correctly linked to smartphone limitations, e.g. reduced motor dexterity or motor impairment making small tap targets on a touchscreen difficult to use accurately (1); OR visual impairment meaning the small smartphone screen and text are hard to read even with zoom (1); OR cognitive accessibility needs meaning the complexity of smartphone apps and notifications is overwhelming (1).

practice_questions.text: Outline why location is an important audience demographic when choosing a distribution channel for a digital communication.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks: urban audiences typically have access to fast broadband and 4G/5G mobile coverage, making data-heavy channels such as HD video streaming viable (1); rural audiences may have slower or less reliable connectivity, so lightweight channels such as email or SMS that function on low-bandwidth connections are more suitable to ensure the communication can actually be received (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe how age as an audience demographic affects the choice of digital device for a campaign targeting primary school children.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks: primary school children (typically aged 4–11) are developing motor skills and have lower dexterity than adults (1); tablets are more suitable than smartphones because the larger screen and bigger touch targets are easier to use accurately, and tablets are commonly used in primary education — children are already familiar with them as learning tools (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain why a national health charity should use email rather than a mobile app to distribute health information to retired adults aged over 70 in rural areas.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (3): demographic identified: the target audience is older adults in rural areas (1); email is suitable because it works on slow broadband connections common in rural areas — the charity cannot assume its audience has high-speed internet (1); additionally, older adults are less likely to own smartphones and may have difficulty installing and navigating apps, whereas email is accessible on a PC or laptop which this demographic is more likely to use and be familiar with (1).
Secure (2): two mark points addressed; one demographic factor linked to channel suitability.
Developing (1): email recommended without linking to demographic characteristics or connectivity constraints.
Emerging (0): no creditworthy content.

practice_questions.text: A local council wants to promote a new recycling scheme to three different audience groups: (1) teenagers aged 13–18 in an urban area, (2) adults aged 60+ in a rural area, and (3) users who are visually impaired. For each group, recommend a suitable digital device and distribution channel. Sketch a matrix showing your recommendations and justifications for each group and demographic factor.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8–9): three groups addressed with device, channel and justification all linked to demographic characteristics. Teenagers/urban: smartphone and mobile app or social media channel — high smartphone ownership, urban 4G coverage, young demographic digitally confident (3); adults 60+/rural: PC/laptop and email — lower smartphone ownership in older demographic, email familiar to this age group on desktop, works on slow rural broadband, large text possible in email client (3); visually impaired users: PC/laptop or tablet and website with accessibility features (screen reader compatibility, adjustable text, high contrast) — larger screen aids low-vision users, desktop screen readers work on websites, email also acceptable if formatted for accessibility (3).
Secure (5–7): all three groups addressed with mostly accurate justifications; one or two demographic links missing.
Developing (3–4): two groups addressed with justification, or three groups without demographic linkage.
Emerging (1–2): one group addressed or devices named without justification.
0: no creditworthy content.

practice_questions.text: Which user interaction method is most suitable for a cook who needs to set a timer while their hands are covered in food?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: voice (only). Distractors: touch (requires clean hands and looking at a screen), keyboard (requires clean dry hands and a surface), mouse (requires a surface and is not hands-free).

practice_questions.text: State one disadvantage of using voice as a user interaction method.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: accept any one valid disadvantage, e.g. voice interaction is unreliable in noisy environments because background sound interferes with recognition (1); OR raises privacy concerns because the device must constantly listen for a wake word (1); OR may not work well for users with speech impairments or strong accents (1).

practice_questions.text: Outline the difference between device-to-device and human-to-device interactivity in the IoE.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks: device-to-device (M2M) interactivity is automated communication between two or more connected devices without human involvement — for example a fitness tracker automatically sending heart rate data to a smartphone app (1); human-to-device interactivity is when a person directly gives instructions to or receives information from a connected device in real time — for example using a voice command to control a smart speaker (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe two advantages and two disadvantages of touch as a user interaction method.
practice_questions.marks: 4 marks, 1 per accurate advantage or disadvantage. Advantages: direct and intuitive — tapping an icon mimics physically pressing a button, requiring no learning of separate input commands (1); requires no separate input device such as a mouse or keyboard, making devices more portable and simpler to use (1). Disadvantages: small interface elements are difficult to tap accurately, particularly for users with reduced motor dexterity (1); prolonged use on a vertical touchscreen (e.g. a smartboard) causes arm fatigue (1). Accept other valid points.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a smart home system uses both device-to-device and human-to-device interactivity, and give one example of each.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (3): defines or clearly implies device-to-device as automated without human involvement — e.g. a smart thermostat automatically reducing heating when a linked door sensor detects the house is empty (1); defines or clearly implies human-to-device as direct user control of a connected device — e.g. a homeowner using a smartphone app to lock the front door (1); explains the relationship: both types of interactivity occur within the same IoE network; the system can act autonomously (M2M) or respond to human commands, giving users both automation and manual control (1).
Secure (2): both types described with accurate examples; link between them underdeveloped.
Developing (1): one type described correctly with an example.
Emerging (0): no creditworthy content.

practice_questions.text: A hospital is designing an HCI for a patient monitoring system used in an intensive care ward. Sketch a comparison of gesture, touch and voice as interaction methods for this context, including advantages, disadvantages and a justified recommendation for each use case in the ward.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8): sketch or structured comparison addresses all three methods in the hospital ICU context. Gesture: may be impractical for medical staff wearing gloves (reduced accuracy on capacitive screens) (1); suitable for navigating large data displays where swipe navigation aids review of patient history (1). Touch: direct and fast for selecting patient profiles and inputting readings (1); hygiene concern — touchscreens in clinical settings must be regularly cleaned; large, clearly labelled targets essential to avoid errors (1). Voice: ideal for hands-free operation when gloved or otherwise occupied (1); unsuitable in noisy ward environments where multiple alarms and conversations cause recognition errors; privacy risk if patient information is spoken aloud (1). Recommendation: justified selection of touch for routine data entry (clean screen protocols, large buttons) plus voice for hands-free alarm dismissal only, with gesture for secondary navigation (1). Explanation of why no single method is universally best in this context (1).
Secure (5–6): two or three methods addressed with context-specific justification; recommendation present.
Developing (3–4): methods listed with generic advantages/disadvantages, limited hospital context.
Emerging (1–2): one method addressed or general description with no context.
0: no creditworthy content.
